title: Client hint budgets — sketch for client-driven latency & fidelity control
content:
Goal:
Quick sketch of a lightweight, client-driven way for applications to signal latency vs fidelity preferences per request so the server can make routing + model-choice decisions and apply graceful degradation. Want something that is backward-compatible with existing Redwood API surface and tiny for clients to opt into (headers or optional request fields).

Problem space / motivation:
- Apps (mobile/web) often have hard UX constraints: some flows need responses under 200ms (search suggestions), others can wait 1–3s (long form summarization).
- Today teams manage by routing entire routes to different models or building client-side heuristics. That's brittle and coarse-grained.
- If client can supply a small "hint" per request, Redwood can do smarter routing: choose low-latency quantized model, enable streaming, or return partial/abridged answers with an explicit fidelity token.
- This can reduce cost (use cheaper model when latency-critical) and improve UX (predictable tail latencies).

Principles:
- Opt-in, non-breaking: default behavior is unchanged if hint absent.
- Small surface area: 1–2 optional headers or request fields.
- Expressive enough for common cases: provide latency budget + fidelity preference + allow server to respond with an explicit contract about what was returned.
- Measurable: instrument per-request routing decision and cost delta.

Candidate API shape (headers):
- X-RW-Latency-Budget-ms: integer (e.g., 150) — tells Redwood the max end-to-end latency client cares about; server will try to satisfy under this SLO or return a graceful fallback.
- X-RW-Fidelity: enum { low | default | high } — preference hint; default if omitted.
- X-RW-Partial-Accept: percent (0–100) — how much of a best-effort partial/abridged answer the client will accept (used for streaming or chunked responses).

Alternative: body fields in request JSON: "client_latency_budget_ms", "client_fidelity" — but headers are easier for existing SDKs and proxies.

Server-side behaviors (examples):
- If latency budget <= 200ms: route to low-latency quantized variant, enable aggressive prefix caching, use shorter generation length defaults, prioritize stream-first path.
- If fidelity=high: route to higher-capacity model (larger context/FP16/less aggressive quantization) and accept higher latency, but if budget conflicts, prefer budget and return an explanatory metadata flag.
- If partial-accept > 0 and model cannot finish within budget: stream an abridged completion with "partial: true" metadata and a short summary token that signals missing content.
- Instrumentation: emit routing_decision, latency_budget_ms, chosen_model_variant, served_latency_ms, cost_estimate_tokens.

Response contract additions (metadata fields):
- _rw_client_hint_applied: true/false
- _rw_routed_variant: "v-quant-8b-lowlatency"
- _rw_served_latency_ms: number
- _rw_partial: true/false
- _rw_explanation: short code/string when budget forced fallback (e.g., "budget_clamped_to_low_variant")

User stories:
- As a mobile dev, I want suggestions to render within 120ms on slow networks, even if they are not perfect, so users can type quickly.
- As an analytics product manager, I want to see how often clients request high fidelity vs low fidelity so we can estimate cost impact.
- As a platform admin, I want an SLA that guarantees 99% of requests with budget<=200ms use the low-latency pool unless capacity-constrained, and when capacity constrained, Redwood must mark requests as degraded and route to fallback region.

Metrics to track (initial):
- percent_requests_with_client_hint
- avg_latency_by_budget_bucket (<=100ms, 100–300ms, >300ms)
- cost_delta_by_hint (cost per request normalized)
- fallback_rate_when_budget_unsatisfiable
- user-visible degradation events (partial responses)

Rollout plan (lightweight experiment):
1) Internal Beta: enable header parsing on a staging tenant + metric dashboard. Test client prototypes in-house with manual routing toggles.
2) Canary: opt-in via account flag for a set of customers (enable debug headers and response metadata).
3) Default-on (opt-out): after 8 weeks of stable metrics and acceptable fallback rates, enable parsing but do not alter default routing unless header present.

Edge cases & open questions:
- Security: could hints be abused to game pricing (spam high-fidelity flags)? Need server-side quotas and tenant-level policy.
- Billing semantics: if client asks high fidelity but we serve low-latency variant due to budget, which price tier applies? (prefer charging for actual served model).
- Abuse/DoS: headers could be set to extreme values; gate by sane ranges and tenant quotas.
- Multi-hop: how do web caches / CDNs treat headers? Need standardization or SDK helpers that sign/attach header near edge.
- UX for devs: lightweight docs + examples in SDK (python/js add header helper).

Concrete next actions (TODOs):
- Spike: implement header parser + routing hook that chooses model variant based on budget bucket (2d effort). Owner: Samir.
- Metrics: add tags to existing request telemetry (Evan/Telemetry team).
- Docs: draft SDK examples and quickstart (Evelyn).
- Design: create short UX copy for response metadata when partial=true (Noah).

Notes to self / rough timeline: 2–4 sprint mini-project to get an internal beta, followed by metrics collection. Keep scope small: start with two budget buckets (<=200ms, >200ms) and three fidelity levels.

References / inspirations:
- browser "Client Hints" pattern (similar lightweight hints to servers)
- adaptive bitrate streaming as analogous pattern (server adapts quality to client constraints)

Unresolved decisions to discuss in sync: billing model, exact header names, and whether to auto-truncate tokens vs stream partial content.

-- end of sketch --
